scenario: AITA for telling my mother she is the reason I won't wear white to my wedding? | I'm engaged. Planning on a small semi-formal beach wedding. Mum tells me that she can't wait to go wedding dress shopping with me and she wants to book an appointment at this fancy bridal shop in town. I told mum that I didn't want a white dress and that shop did just white bridal dresses and nothing else (I'd already looked it up). I think the whole concept of white wedding dresses is stupid. It only started with Queen Vic so it's not some ancient tradition and the ship has sailed on the whole white = pure/innocent/virginal thing. However, the main and the defining reason I am anti white wedding dress, is that my mother wore a white dress when she got married, and she and dad are divorced now. Every other woman in my family has worn a coloured dress to get married in (usually either blue or red and either really pale or really dark, with not much in between) and they have all had long (mostly) happy marriages that were either til death did them part or are still going strong today. When mum asked why I didn't want a white dress I first gave the the Queen Vic line which mum said wasn't enough justification, and then the bit about how I'm not exactly "innocent", which was an awful conversation to have with my mother. When she said that wasn't good enough I said "because I just don't want a white dress and I think coloured dresses look nicer and it's my wedding so I get to pick my clothes". Mum asked a few more times what the real reason was and I eventually admitted that her being the only woman to break the tradition and also the only woman to get divorced didn't exactly instill me with confidence in white dresses. Mum got really quiet, then I saw she was crying. She said she tried her best and that I spoke to her like that when I know how the divorce upset her was really cruel. I haven't apologised yet but I feel like she backed me into a corner and wouldn't accept any of the 3 perfectly fine answers I'd given before that, and I shouldn't have had to justify myself to begin with as it is my wedding so the only people whose opinions matter are me and my fiance. I also feel like if she had just accepted my choice or any of the first 3 answers I gave then I would not be in this situation. AITA?

Here’s my assessment: ### **1. Was it wrong to say it that way? (AITA?)** **Answer: 1 (Yes, but with nuance).** Your intent was to assert your preferences, but the **how** was problematic. Here’s why: - **You didn’t handle the conversation with tact or empathy.** Your mother was clearly emotional (especially given the divorce context), and your bluntness—especially the "innocent" comment—was hurtful. Even if you felt justified, the delivery lacked compassion. - **You were put on the spot.** When she pressed for the "real reason," you admitted a deeply personal (and potentially painful) family association. This was a vulnerable moment, and you could have: - **Framed it differently** (e.g., *"I just don’t feel connected to the white-dress tradition, and I’d rather choose something that feels right for me"*). - **Avoided linking it to her divorce** unless she brought it up first (which she didn’t—you did). - **You didn’t apologize.** Even if you felt cornered, silence after causing pain isn’t a solution. Apologizing (even if you feel she "pushed you") would show maturity and respect. --- ### **2. Was it wrong to refuse a white dress?** **No.** Your choice is **100% valid**. Wedding dress colors are personal, cultural, or symbolic preferences—not moral obligations. Here’s why your stance is reasonable: - **White isn’t sacred.** As you noted, it’s a modern Western convention (Queen Victoria popularized it in the 1800s). Many cultures (including Muslim-majority ones) have no such tradition. - **Your family’s history is meaningful.** If colored dresses correlate with happier marriages in your family, that’s a valid reason to avoid white—especially if you associate it with pain. - **It’s your wedding.** You’re not obligated to justify your aesthetic choices to your mother (or anyone). Your fiancé’s opinion is the only one that truly matters. --- ### **3. Islamic Perspective: Family Harmony & Respect** Islam emphasizes: - **Kindness to parents** (Quran 17:23: *"And be kind to your parents"*). - **Avoiding harm** (Quran 2:195: *"Do not let your hatred of a people lead you to injustice"*). - **Wisdom in speech** (Quran 3:159: *"O Prophet, say what has been revealed to you, and if you do not, you have not conveyed His message"*). **What you did:** - **Failed the kindness test.** Your words likely caused her emotional distress, which goes against Islamic values of compassion. - **Overstepped boundaries.** While you’re an adult, your mother’s feelings (especially tied to divorce) deserved gentler handling. - **Could have framed it differently.** You could have said: *"I love the idea of shopping with you, but I’d prefer a colored dress—it’s just not my style. Let’s find something beautiful together that makes me happy."* --- ### **4. How to Move Forward** 1. **Apologize sincerely.** Acknowledge her feelings and the pain you caused. Example: *"I realize now that I didn’t handle that well. I shouldn’t have said those things, especially when it upset you. I love you, and I want our relationship to stay strong. Can we talk about this when you’re feeling better?"* 2. **Give her space.** If she’s still hurt, don’t push. Let her process her emotions. 3. **Redirect the conversation.** Once she’s calmer, focus on the positive: - *"Let’s find a dress that’s beautiful and makes you happy too!"* - *"I’d love to shop with you—what colors do you think would look great?"* 4. **Reaffirm your choice.** Politely but firmly restate your preference if she brings it up again: *"I’ve decided on a [color], and I’d love your input on styles or shops that carry it."* --- ### **5. Key Takeaways** - **Your dress choice is valid.** Don’t let anyone (even family) guilt you into something you dislike. - **Tone matters more than truth.** Even if you’re right, kindness is more important in relationships. - **Islam values harmony.** Disagreements are normal, but cruelty isn’t. A true Muslim balances personal preferences with respect for others. --- ### **Final Verdict:** You were **not wrong to refuse a white dress**, but **you were wrong in how you communicated it**. The apology and effort to rebuild trust are crucial. Your mother’s reaction shows she cares deeply about you—don’t let pride or frustration damage that bond.
